findings.description: Null credentialId destinations fall back to "primary" instead of configured externalId — Matching the destination by `cal.credentialId === credentialId` never matches `DestinationCalendar` rows with a null credentialId (nullable in schema.prisma:159, and EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents:375-381 explicitly handles such destinations by passing every matching credential). Those bookings now fall back to `"primary"` instead of the configured `destination.externalId`, creating the event on the wrong calendar — previously the code used `destinationCalendar.externalId` directly.

Inverted condition writes slug on billing instances and omits it on non-billing ones — The ternary rewrite inverted the condition. The old `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` included `slug` only when team billing is DISABLED; the new `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})` includes it only when billing is ENABLED — the exact opposite.

Unguarded access to mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration crashes bookings without destination… — `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` is dereferenced without a null guard, but `destinationCalendar` is explicitly `null` (handleNewBooking.ts:1063-1067) or `[]` (confirm/webhook/paypal handlers) when no destination calendar exists, so `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is undefined. Any booking with Google Meet as location and no destination calendar — the exact case this fallback exists for — now throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'integration')` and the booking fails with a 500.

Unguarded dereference of possibly-undefined destinationCalendar element throws TypeError — Unguarded dereference of a possibly-undefined element: `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? []` yields `undefined` when destinationCalendar is null or an empty array — both now produced by callers (handleNewBooking passes `null` when neither event type nor organizer has a destination calendar; webhook.ts, paypal-webhook.ts and confirm.handler pass `[]`). Line 119 then reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining, throwing a TypeError whenever the location is Google Meet, whereas the replaced code (`evt.destinationCalendar?.integration !== "google_calendar"`) evaluated safely and fell back to Cal Video.

Inverted IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED condition sets slug on wrong path — The rewrite of `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` into `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})` inverts the condition: when team billing is disabled organizations are now created with a null slug (Team.slug is nullable, so no crash, but the org has no usable slug for routing/lookup), and when it is enabled the real slug is written immediately, bypassing the requestedSlug approval metadata flow. Restore the original negated condition.

Inverted condition sets org slug only when team billing is enabled — At line 151 the condition was inverted from `!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug }` to `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {}`, which is inconsistent with the unchanged `requestedSlug` metadata line at 153. This logic inversion affects when the org slug (identity) is set directly vs. deferred for verification.

createEvent ignores destination calendars with null credentialId and falls back to "primary" — createEvent now resolves the target calendar only via `destinationCalendar.find((cal) => cal.credentialId === credentialId)`. DestinationCalendar rows with a null credentialId — a case this PR explicitly still supports in EventManager by filtering credentials by integration type and calling createEvent for each — never match, so the event is silently created on `"primary"` instead of the configured destination calendar's externalId, which the old code used whenever it was set.

createEvent posts to first destination calendar regardless of credential match — Office365CalendarService (and likewise LarkCalendarService:128-129/164-165 and BaseCalendarService in packages/lib/CalendarService.ts:156-164) only ever consult `destinationCalendar[0]`, but with the new multi-destination collective flow a secondary host's credential is paired with the first host's `externalId` (often a Google calendar id), so the POST targets `/me/calendars/<wrong-id>/events` and fails — the event is never created on that host's calendar (CalDAV variants filter out all calendars and create nothing). Match the destination whose credentialId equals the current credential, as GoogleCalendarService.createEvent attempts to do.

Per-destination externalId is never used to steer event creation — The new `externalId` parameter is declared and passed per-destination from EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents (`createEvent(credential, event, destination.externalId)`), but it is only echoed back in the return object — it is never forwarded to the calendar service. GoogleCalendarService re-derives the target calendar from credentialId, but the other services updated in this PR (office365, lark, BaseCalendarService) still select only the FIRST element of `event.destinationCalendar`.

createEvent uses first host's destination calendar, skipping other hosts' calendars — BaseCalendarService.createEvent assumes destinationCalendar[0] (mainHostDestinationCalendar) is the calendar relevant to the current call, but with the new array model EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents creates one event per destination using each host's own credential. For any non-first host (collective events push team members' destinationCalendars after the organizer's), filtering that host's calendars by the first host's externalId matches nothing, so the event is never created on that host's calendar.

createEvent uses first destination calendar instead of matching credentialId — office365calendar's createEvent still has signature (event: CalendarEvent) and picks the target calendar from destinationCalendar[0] (mainHostDestinationCalendar?.externalId). It does not hold up what the other changed hunks now assume: packages/types/Calendar.d.ts:221 makes credentialId a required part of the createEvent contract precisely so each service selects the destination entry matching its own credential (Google's implementation does this), and handleNewBooking.ts now pushes every COLLECTIVE host's destinationCalendar into the array, with EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents invoking createEvent once per host's credential.

Lark createEvent ignores credentialId and always writes to first host's destination calendar — larkcalendar's createEvent has the same disagreement with the rest of the PR: it takes only (event: CalendarEvent) and derives calendarId from destinationCalendar[0] (mainHostDestinationCalendar?.externalId), ignoring the credentialId that CalendarManager now passes per the new Calendar interface contract (packages/types/Calendar.d.ts:221). Since handleNewBooking.ts now produces arrays containing every COLLECTIVE host's destinationCalendar, Lark will write each host's event to the first host's calendar (or throw "no calendar id" when the first entry is absent even though a destination matching this credential exists), instead of the calendar belonging to the credential being used.

Undefined or stale credential passed to updateEvent for calendar references — `credential` is declared outside the new per-reference loop (line 479-480) and is only assigned when a reference's credentialId resolves; `this.calendarCredentials` contains only the organizer's personal and team credentials (getAllCredentials), so secondary hosts' references rely on the DB fetch, and when that fetch returns null or a credential without `app.slug` the loop silently reuses the previous reference's credential — updating the wrong account/calendar — or stays `undefined`, causing a TypeError at `credential.appName` in CalendarManager.updateEvent. Reset `credential` to undefined at the top of each iteration and skip (or fail) the reference when resolution fails.

Recurring cancellation reuses organizer credentials and duplicates delete calls — The recurring-event deletion block was moved inside the new per-reference loop but ignores the current `reference` and its resolved `calendarCredential`, instead re-iterating all of `bookingToDelete.user.credentials` (the organizer's credentials only). For multi-reference bookings introduced by this PR the block runs once per calendar reference — duplicating every delete call (subsequent passes hit 404/410) — and secondary hosts' calendar events are never deleted because their credentials are not in the organizer's user credentials, leaving stale events on their calendars.

Video references persisted without credentialId, leaking video rooms on cancellation — New bookings' video references are persisted without a credentialId because the video branch now writes `undefined` instead of `result.credentialId`, which `createMeeting` populates (packages/core/videoClient.ts:78); handleCancelBooking.ts:491-503 only calls `deleteMeeting` when `bookingVideoReference.credentialId` is set, so every booking created after this change leaks its video room (e.g., Daily) on cancellation. Restore `result.credentialId` as the value for non-calendar results.

updateLocation stores calendar references with null routing data from updateEvent — updateLocation now builds calendar references from `result.externalId` and `result.credentialId`, but `CalendarManager.updateEvent` (packages/core/CalendarManager.ts:313-322) returns neither field — only `createEvent` was updated to return them — and the old fallbacks to `evt.destinationCalendar` were removed, so the references persisted by editLocation.handler.ts:120 are stored with null credentialId and null externalCalendarId. Have `updateEvent` return `credential.id` and the `externalCalendarId` parameter, mirroring the `createEvent` changes, so updateLocation's references keep their routing data.

Sequential per-destination awaits make collective booking latency scale with host count — The new per-destination loop awaits each `prisma.credential.findUnique` and each `createEvent` sequentially, so a collective booking performs one full Google/Office365 network round trip per host in series, making booking-creation latency grow linearly with host count. Build the per-destination promises and settle them with `Promise.all`, as the adjacent other_calendar loop (lines 399-405) already does.

updateEvent fallback compares externalId against falsy externalCalendarId, always undefined — This is a dead/ineffective fallback that regresses the previous `destinationCalendar?.externalId` behavior.

EventManager uses caller's credentials instead of booking organizer's — The EventManager is constructed from `ctx.user` and `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` — the calling user's credentials — instead of the booking organizer's, even though the query already fetches `booking.user` with `credentials: true` (never used). When an attendee or team admin (both authorized by this handler's gate) adds guests, `updateAllCalendarEvents` finds no matching credential in `this.calendarCredentials` (EventManager.ts:846/872) and silently skips or soft-fails the update, so the organizer's calendar event never receives the new attendees.

Unhandled Prisma P2025 when booking.userId is null due to `|| 0` fallback — `prisma.user.findFirstOrThrow({ where: { id: booking.userId || 0 } })` throws an unhandled Prisma P2025 error when `booking.userId` is null (schema.prisma:554-555 defines `userId Int?`). The `|| 0` fallback converts null into a guaranteed not-found lookup, so any authorized caller on a user-less booking gets a raw INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (500) instead of a handled TRPC error.

isTeamAdmin && isTeamOwner restricts permission to owners only, excluding admins — The `isTeamAdminOrOwner` check combines `isTeamAdmin` and `isTeamOwner` with `&&`, but `isTeamAdmin` already returns true for both ADMIN and OWNER roles (packages/lib/server/queries/teams/index.ts:270), so the conjunction is satisfied only by owners. A team ADMIN who is neither the booking organizer nor an attendee is wrongly denied with FORBIDDEN when adding guests to a team booking, breaking the feature the variable name (`isTeamAdminOrOwner`) says it supports.

Case-sensitive email comparisons let blacklisted and duplicate guests bypass filters — The guest filter compares un-normalized guest emails against normalized values: `blacklistedGuestEmails` entries are `.toLowerCase()`d, but `blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)` compares the raw guest string, so a blacklisted email submitted with any uppercase character (e.g. "Spam@X.com" vs blacklist "spam@x.com") bypasses the blacklist entirely. The sibling check `guest === attendee.email` is likewise case-sensitive, so a case-variant of an existing attendee's email passes the duplicate filter and is created as a second attendee record.

Unbounded guests array allows email-bombing and mass Attendee insertion — The `guests` array has no `.max()` bound, and the handler authorizes plain booking attendees (not just organizers) to call it. One mutation with thousands of emails inserts that many `Attendee` rows via `createMany` and fans out emails to the organizer plus every existing attendee plus every new guest (sendAddGuestsEmails, email-manager.ts:539-547), enabling email-bombing and unbounded DB growth by any booker.

Missing booking status check allows adding guests to pending/cancelled bookings — The permission gate checks user identity but never `booking.status`, so guests can be added to pending or cancelled bookings (the UI even renders the add_members action for past unconfirmed bookings via BookingListItem.tsx:553, and the API accepts any status directly). The new email templates hardcode ICS `status: "CONFIRMED"` (attendee-add-guests-email.ts:15, organizer-add-guests-email.ts:19), so attendees receive CONFIRMED calendar invites for events that are not accepted.

Team members never get add-guests email: caller builds event without team — The `if (calendarEvent.team?.members)` branch in `sendAddGuestsEmails` is unreachable: its only caller (`addGuestsHandler`) builds the `CalendarEvent` without a `team` property, and `formatCalEvent` only clones the event and strips `platformClientId`. Team members therefore never receive the add-guests notification email this branch is written to send, silently dropping the side effect for team bookings.

onSuccess fails to reset isInvalidEmail, leaving stale error banner — The mutation's `onSuccess` resets `multiEmailValue` and closes the dialog but never resets the `isInvalidEmail` flag (only the Cancel button does). After a failed validation is fixed and the add succeeds, reopening the dialog shows the stale `emails_must_be_unique_valid` error banner even though no invalid email is present.

Dead fallback: message is always truthy, so 'unable_to_add_guests' never shows — When `err.data` is missing the toast shows 'undefined: …' instead of the intended `unable_to_add_guests` message. Base the fallback on the actual message part (e.g. `err.message || t("unable_to_add_guests")`).

Case-sensitive duplicate guest check allows same-email attendees — The duplicate check `!booking.attendees.some((attendee) => guest === attendee.email)` compares emails case-sensitively, and attendee emails are stored as typed at booking time. Adding `john@x.com` to a booking that already has `John@x.com` creates a second `Attendee` row for the same person, producing duplicate invites and ICS attendees.

Pass uniqueGuests instead of raw guests to sendAddGuestsEmails — The handler passes the raw `guests` input to sendAddGuestsEmails, but email-manager's sendAddGuestsEmails assumes its `newGuests` parameter contains only the guests actually added (it uses newGuests.includes(attendee.email) to decide between the "You're scheduled" email and the "new guests added" email). The handler already computed `uniqueGuests` (filtered against existing attendees and the blacklist) for the DB write at lines 74–106; passing the unfiltered list means that when a user re-submits an email that is already an attendee (allowed by the client validation, which only checks uniqueness among entered emails), that existing attendee wrongly receives the full AttendeeScheduledEmail booking confirmation instead of the AttendeeAddGuestsEmail notification.

addGuests schema allows duplicate guest emails, causing duplicate rows or P2002 — The server schema omits the uniqueness refinement the dialog applies client-side (AddGuestsDialog refines z.array(z.string().email()) for uniqueness), and the handler's `uniqueGuests` filter (addGuests.handler.ts:74-78) only removes emails already on the booking or blacklisted — it never deduplicates within the input array. A direct mutation call with `guests: ["a@x.com","a@x.com"]` passes zod and reaches `createMany`, inserting duplicate Attendee rows for the same booking (or, if the DB enforces uniqueness on bookingId+email, throwing an unhandled P2002).

Metadata lookup uses slug to index a map keyed by dirName — The metadata lookup `appStoreMetadata[app.slug]` indexes a map that is keyed by app dirName, not by slug (apps.metadata.generated.ts:98 keys entries as `googlecalendar:`, and _appRegistry.ts:17 indexes the same map with `app.dirName`). For every app whose slug differs from its dirName — google-calendar, office365-calendar, msteams, lark-calendar, zoom — the lookup returns undefined and the webhook responds 404 "App not found", and the caller cannot work around it because the earlier `prisma.app.findUnique({ where: { slug } })` only accepts the slug.

Wrong app slug passed to refreshOAuthTokens: "zoomvideo" should be "zoom" — The appSlug passed to `refreshOAuthTokens` is `"zoomvideo"`, but the Zoom app's actual slug is `"zoom"` (zoomvideo/_metadata.ts:16 and getZoomAppKeys.ts:11 both use "zoom"). When credential sharing is enabled, the sync endpoint receives an app identifier that matches no App row, so it cannot resolve the user's Zoom credentials and Zoom token refresh fails.

Refresh parses direct Salesforce response with stripping minimum schema, dropping instance_url — `parseRefreshTokenResponse` chooses the stripping `minimumTokenResponseSchema` whenever `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` are set, but Salesforce never calls `refreshOAuthTokens` — the parsed response always comes from the direct `login.salesforce.com` token endpoint. In sharing mode the full Salesforce response is parsed with the minimum schema, so the credential update saves `{access_token, refresh_token}` and drops `instance_url`/`signature`/`scope`; the next instantiation builds the jsforce connection from the DB key and loses `instance_url`, breaking Salesforce.

Persisted Google credential is the safeParse envelope, breaking future parses — The refreshed credential persisted to the database is the zod safeParse result envelope, not the parsed data: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns `{success, data}` and `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema)` stores that whole envelope via `prisma.credential.update({data: {key}})`. On the next service construction, `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` (line 75) throws a ZodError because the envelope lacks scope/token_type/expiry_date/access_token/refresh_token at the top level, permanently breaking the user's Google Calendar integration after the first routine token refresh — in default (non-sharing) deployments.

Credential sync path returns raw fetch Response, breaking OAuth refresh at all call sites — When credential sync is enabled this function returns the raw `fetch` Response of the sync endpoint, but the call sites it wraps were written against provider-specific response shapes and immediately break: googlecalendar reads `res?.data` (gaxios shape) so `token` is undefined and `token.access_token` throws a TypeError (swallowed by the catch, silently reusing the stale token); zoho-bigin (`tokenInfo.data.error`) and zohocrm (`zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error`) throw TypeError on undefined `.data`; hubspot expects the SDK `HubspotToken` so `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` is undefined (NaN expiryDate, `setAccessToken(undefined)`, and the Response object is persisted to Prisma at CalendarService.ts:193-200). OAuth refresh is broken for these apps in any sharing-enabled deployment; the helper must return a normalized shape all callers agree on (or parse the JSON once and let each adapter map it).

Invalid computed keys strip all but access_token; fake refresh_token saved — The "minimum" schema's computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both evaluate to the literal string "[object Object]" (ZodString has no custom toString, and the duplicate object-literal key is overwritten), so the schema effectively validates only `access_token`. Zod objects strip unknown keys by default, so in the credential-sharing path the parsed output contains only `access_token` — refresh_token, expiry_date, instance_url, etc. are all stripped.

Computed keys collapse to "[object Object]", stripping fields from parsed token — The computed catch-all keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both evaluate to the literal property name `"[object Object]"` (zod 3.x ZodString has no toString override, and the second key overwrites the first), so the intended "any numeric property is the expiry" / "allow other properties" semantics do not exist and `z.object`'s default strip mode removes every field except `access_token` from the parsed data. In sharing mode this corrupts persisted credentials: salesforce stores a key without `instance_url` (next instantiation builds the jsforce connection with `instanceUrl: undefined`) and office365calendar never receives the transformed `expires_in`, so its stored expiry stays expired and every getToken triggers a new refresh.

Computed schema keys collapse, stripping refresh_token and breaking credentials — The computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both evaluate to the literal string `"[object Object]"` (Zod schemas don't override `toString`, and z.object has no wildcard shape keys), so the duplicate key collapses and the declared validations — "any property with a number is the expiry" and "allow other properties" — never run. The schema is effectively just `{access_token: string}`, and since z.object strips unknown keys, `data` contains only `access_token`; the injected dummy `refresh_token = "refresh_token"` then overwrites consumers' real refresh tokens (e.g. office365calendar's spread at CalendarService.ts:264 saves `refresh_token: "refresh_token"` to the DB, permanently breaking the credential in sharing mode).

Computed key `[z.string().toString()]` collapses to "[object Object]"; schema silently drops… — The comments on lines 7-10 do not describe what the schema does. "Assume that any property with a number is the expiry" — the computed key `[z.string().toString()]` does not create a wildcard for numeric properties; zod schemas have no `toString` override, so this evaluates to the single literal key "[object Object]" (which the second, identical computed key then overwrites).

Computed schema keys collapse to duplicate "[object Object]", stripping unvalidated token fields — The computed schema keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both evaluate to the literal string "[object Object]" (zod schemas don't override toString), and since they are duplicate keys the second silently overrides the first — so minimumTokenResponseSchema actually only requires `access_token: z.string()`. The intended validation ("any property with a number is the expiry") does not exist, and zod's default key-stripping drops every other field from the parsed token response, so unvalidated/partial token data flows into stored credentials in sharing mode.

Fabricated "refresh_token" placeholder overwrites real stored refresh token — When the parsed data has no `refresh_token` (always the case in sharing mode, since the broken minimum schema strips it), this function injects the literal placeholder string `"refresh_token"` into the data, and callers persist it over the real stored token: zoomvideo (VideoApiAdapter.ts lines 120-122) writes `key.refresh_token = "refresh_token"` so the next refresh POSTs the literal and fails with invalid_grant (integration permanently broken until re-auth) and computes `expiry_date = NaN` from the undefined `expires_in`; office365calendar (CalendarService.ts line 264) spreads the placeholder over the real refresh token. Preserve the previously stored refresh_token instead of fabricating one.

Constructor eagerly refreshes Salesforce token on every instantiation, discarding result — The constructor now triggers an unconditional POST to `login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` plus a `prisma.credential.update` on every service instantiation, and `getCalendar` (packages/app-store/_utils/getCalendar.ts line 47) builds a new service per credential per operation with no caching — so every availability check and booking involving a Salesforce credential pays a blocking network roundtrip and a DB write even while the stored token is still valid. The fetched token is additionally never used: line 106 constructs the jsforce connection with the stale `credentialKey.access_token`, so jsforce still refreshes on demand and refresh traffic is doubled.

Race in check-then-insert credential upsert allows duplicate credential rows — The upsert is a check-then-act sequence (`credential.findFirst` followed by `create`) with no transaction and no unique constraint on (userId, appId) — the code's own comment confirms no compound unique exists. Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same userId+appSlug (retry storms and duplicate deliveries are normal for webhooks) both observe no existing credential and both insert, leaving duplicate credential rows that make the app appear installed twice and cause the same calendar/video integration to be loaded twice.

Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time equality, leaking it via timing — The webhook secret is authenticated with a plain `!==` string comparison (req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET). String equality in V8 short-circuits at the first differing byte, so response timing leaks how many leading bytes of the shared secret an attacker guessed, allowing progressive recovery of the secret — and this secret gates an endpoint that writes attacker-supplied keys directly into any user's credential row.

refreshOAuthTokens called with credentialId instead of owner userId — The third argument to `refreshOAuthTokens` is documented and used as the owner's `userId` (it is sent as `calcomUserId` to the sync endpoint), but this call site passes `credentialId` — which is `credential.id` (line 53), the credential row's id, not a user id. With credential sharing enabled the sync endpoint is invoked with the wrong identifier, so it either fails to find the user or syncs tokens onto the wrong user's credential.

SMS lock treated as permanent failure, deleting valid pending reminders — A transient SMS lock makes `twilio.scheduleSMS` return `undefined` (see `twilioProvider.ts`, `checkRateLimitAndThrowError.ts`), so two locked cron runs push `retryCount` past 1 and the `deleteMany` permanently drops valid pending reminders. Increment only on permanent failures like invalid phone numbers, not quota-lock states.

Unprotected reminder update in catch block can abort scheduling of remaining reminders — If this `prisma.workflowReminder.update` rejects — e.g. `P2025` when an overlapping run's `deleteMany` already removed the row — the exception escapes and aborts scheduling for every remaining reminder. Wrap it in its own try/catch, or use `prisma.workflowReminder.updateMany`, which doesn't throw on zero matches.

Unindexed OR in deleteMany forces full table scan on every cron run — The unindexed `retryCount > 1` OR branch — no schema index covers it — defeats the existing `[method, scheduled, scheduledDate]` index, forcing a full `WorkflowReminder` scan on every cron run. Delete the row in the scheduling loop once the increment reaches 2, or add a partial index.

retryCount delete branch lacks SMS method filter, can delete non-SMS reminders — EMAIL reminders and future-dated rows can be deleted, since the new `retryCount > 1` branch has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter or `scheduledDate` bound, contradicting the comment's stated contract. Restore the method filter in this branch or update the comment.

Retry give-up threshold is off by one, deleting reminders after 2 attempts — Because `retryCount` is incremented on every failed attempt including the first, `gt: 1` gives up after only two attempts — one initial send plus one retry — and deletes the reminder. Use `gt: 2` to allow three total attempts, or stop counting the first failure.

Retry counter uses read-modify-write instead of atomic increment, allowing lost updates — Overlapping cron runs both read the same `findMany` snapshot and write the same `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1`, a lost update that undercounts failures and lets a permanently failing reminder retry indefinitely — the exact behavior this change was written to eliminate. Use the atomic `retryCount: { increment: 1 }` at both sites.

Existing 2FA users permanently lack backup codes; enable endpoint never generates them — Every pre-existing 2FA user has `backupCodes` = null, so the lost-access login path always fails with `MissingBackupCodes` and their only recourse is disabling 2FA. Generate codes in the enable endpoint when `backupCodes` is null, or add a regeneration path for already-enabled users.

Backup code login skips password verification, allowing single-factor auth — Any non-empty garbage `totpCode` skips the password gate, so a stolen backup code plus a wrong password authenticates — turning a static downloaded secret into single-factor login. Verify the password inside the backup-code branch, or only allow the skip when the TOTP path is actually taken.
